title: Given a `List<Employee>`, produce a `Map<String, List<String>>` of department to the list of employee names in that department, using `groupingBy` with a `Collectors.mapping` downstream.
shortTitle: Group employees by department, then collect only employee names per department using Collectors.mapping

s1_definition.profdef: `Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream)` adapts a collector by applying a mapping function to each element before passing it to the downstream collector. As the downstream of `groupingBy`, `mapping(Employee::getName, toList())` transforms each grouped Employee into its name and collects the names into a list, giving `Map<String, List<String>>`.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants, per department, just the list of names, not the full staff cards. So as each card drops into a department tray, she writes down only the person's name and keeps a slip of names per tray. The mapping downstream is "before you store it, convert the card to just a name".
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, mapping(getName, toList()))` collects just the names per department.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.mapping(mapper, downstream)` adapts a collector by applying a mapping function to each element before passing it to the downstream collector. As the downstream of `groupingBy`, `mapping(Employee::getName, toList())` transforms each grouped Employee into its name and collects the names into a list, giving `Map<String, List<String>>`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants, per department, just the list of names, not the full staff cards. So as each card drops into a department tray, she writes down only the person's name and keeps a slip of names per tray. The mapping downstream is "before you store it, convert the card to just a name".

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(dept, mapping(getName, toList()))` collects just the names per department.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collectors.mapping` is an adapting collector: it takes a mapper and a downstream collector, applies the mapper to each incoming element, and feeds the mapped value to the downstream. It is the collector-level equivalent of a `map` followed by a collect, but it happens inside the grouping, per group.

Used as the groupingBy downstream, `mapping(Employee::getName, Collectors.toList())` means "for each department group, convert every Employee to its name and gather the names into a list". So IT with Rajesh and Amit becomes "IT" mapped to ["Rajesh", "Amit"].

Why not just `map` on the stream before grouping? Because once you map Employees to names up front you lose the department, so you can no longer group by it. `Collectors.mapping` solves this by keeping the grouping on the full Employee and only reducing to the name inside each group. A senior extension: you can nest further, for example `mapping(Employee::getName, toCollection(TreeSet::new))` to get sorted, de-duplicated names per department.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India prints a department roster that shows only staff names under each department heading, not the full records. Grouping the whole Employee objects and then extracting names afterwards is clumsy. This is exactly how `Collectors.mapping` works — it reduces each grouped Employee to just its name while still grouping by department.

Problem 2 — The roster must not lose the department grouping. This is exactly why mapping is applied as a downstream rather than mapping the stream first, which would discard the department key.

The code defines `Employee`, a `RosterService` with `namesByDepartment`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT, Priya Finance, Amit IT, Sneha Finance.

Step 1: Grouping keys each employee by department: IT and Finance groups form.

Step 2: Inside the IT group, mapping converts Rajesh and Amit to their names "Rajesh" and "Amit" and collects them into a list.

Step 3: Inside Finance, mapping collects "Priya" and "Sneha".

Step 4: The TreeMap yields alphabetical keys, each mapped to its name list.

```
INFO: Finance -> [Priya, Sneha]
INFO: IT -> [Rajesh, Amit]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh/IT, Priya/Finance, Amit/IT, Sneha/Finance]
    │ groupingBy(dept, mapping(getName, toList()))
    ▼
  group by dept (keep full Employee for the key)
    ├─ IT      → [Rajesh, Amit]  --mapping(getName)--> ["Rajesh","Amit"]
    └─ Finance → [Priya, Sneha]  --mapping(getName)--> ["Priya","Sneha"]
    ▼
  TreeMap<String,List<String>>
    ▼
  Output: {Finance:["Priya","Sneha"], IT:["Rajesh","Amit"]}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To collect just the names per department I use `groupingBy` with `Collectors.mapping(Employee::getName, Collectors.toList())` as the downstream. mapping is an adapting collector: it applies a mapper to each element before handing it to the downstream, so inside each department group every Employee is converted to its name and the names are gathered into a list, giving a Map of department to a list of names.

The key insight I always explain is why I do not simply map the stream to names before grouping. If I mapped Employees to names first, I would throw away the department, and then I could not group by it. `Collectors.mapping` solves exactly this: it keeps the grouping on the full Employee object and only reduces to the name inside each group.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this produced a department roster that printed just the staff names under each department heading. I mention that the same pattern extends naturally, for instance using `mapping(Employee::getName, toCollection(TreeSet::new))` when I want the names per department sorted and de-duplicated, which shows how composable the downstream collectors are.
